FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–6 YEARS

Kitchen Things flashcards.

Thirty-five cards that name the busiest room in the house, sorted into age pills so parents know exactly what is on the menu: the everyday things a three-year-old already uses, the helper tools a four- or five-year-old can start with, the grown-up tools older kids love to name and one card — the chef’s knife — that exists to teach the kitchen’s biggest rule: knives are for grown-ups. The class game is Kitchen Helper: find the item, say its name, then sort the cards into "I can use it" and "grown-ups only."

THE CARDS

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page, and every card shows its age pill — start with the group that fits your child today.

Ages 3 and up

The everyday kitchen kids see every day and can already use: spoon, fork, plate, mug, bowl, kettle, fridge, microwave, toaster, trash bin — plus the pans and the dishwasher.

Ages 4–5

The helper tools: whisk, rolling pin, ladle, spatula, colander, measuring cup and spoons, oven mitt, timer, tongs — the real baking and stirring kit.

Ages 6 and up

The grown-up tools: kids this young don’t use them, but they are fine as "what is this?" cards — garlic press, mortar and pestle, box grater, funnel, strainer, food thermometer, peeler, coffee maker and blender.

Grown-ups only

One card, one rule: knives are for grown-ups. The chef’s knife stays on the shelf so the kitchen’s biggest safety rule can be taught, not hidden.

Chef’s KnifeCard 4 of 35Grown-ups onlyKnives are for grown-ups
HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Play Kitchen Helper

    The class game in three steps: the child finds the item, says its name, then sorts the card into one of two piles — "I can use it" and "grown-ups only." The sorting IS the safety lesson, and every child’s piles are a little different, which makes a great family conversation.

  2. 02

    Follow the age pills

    Every card carries an age pill. Start with the Ages 3+ cards, graduate to the helper tools at four or five, and let the Ages 6+ cards stay a name-only game until small hands are ready. Nothing needs to be rushed — the pills do the pacing.

  3. 03

    Run the hot-check

    Spread the cards face up and ask: which ones get HOT? The kettle, the saucepan, the frying pan, the baking tray, the microwave, the toaster. Every hot card gets a toy oven mitt dropped on it — a sorting game that teaches the kitchen’s most important rule while it plays.

  4. 04

    Cook one real thing

    Pick the simplest helper card — measuring cups in banana muffins, a whisk in pancake batter, a rolling pin on cookie dough — and cook it together. The card names the tool, the kitchen uses the tool, and the recipe does the rest.
